claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy is a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution.
The initial alloy has high ductility and toughness under standard or low-to-moderate loading conditions.
The initial alloy exhibits ductile fracture under low-to-moderate loading conditions.
Severe mechanical loading causes localized microstructural evolution in the alloy.
The loading-induced microstructural evolution produces nanoscale precipitates or ordered regions.
The nanoscale precipitates or ordered regions form preferentially at grain boundaries and along dislocation arrays.
High mechanical loading increases local stresses and dislocation activity.
Loading-induced local stresses and dislocation activity drive nucleation of nanoscale brittle phases through solute segregation or partial phase separation.
The resulting precipitates, ordered regions, or brittle phases hinder plastic deformation.
The loading-induced microstructural changes reduce fracture toughness.
The loading-induced microstructural changes shift fracture behavior from ductile to brittle.
Severely loaded specimens will show nanoscale precipitates or ordered regions detectable by TEM, SEM, XRD, or elemental mapping.
Severely loaded specimens will show brittle-fracture features such as cleavage facets.
The proposed loss of toughness and brittle transition occur only above loading and temperature conditions sufficient to activate local microstructural evolution.
Under milder loading conditions, the alloy retains ductile behavior.
The critical load and temperature thresholds depend on alloy composition and testing environment.
A controlled comparison uses identical specimens, with one set subjected to severe loading and another retained under baseline conditions.
Failure to observe a statistically significant toughness reduction, new precipitates or ordering, or a brittle-fracture transition would falsify the proposed mechanism.
